vignette: At 71 years old, Gus had always taken pride in his work as a security guard. He had spent decades keeping people safe, and it was a job he took very seriously. But that all changed on the day of the terrorist attack at the mall where he worked. Gus was one of the first responders to the scene, and what he saw would stay with him forever. As he recounted the events of that day, Gus's memories were vivid and clear. He remembered the sound of gunfire, the screams of the people running for cover, and the smell of smoke filling the air. But when he talked about it, his voice was flat and emotionless, as if he was describing something that had happened to someone else. Sometimes, he couldn't even put the events into a coherent story - it was all just fragments of chaos. In the months following the attack, Gus began to notice changes in himself. He became hypervigilant, always on the lookout for potential dangers lurking around every corner. When he sat down, whether at home or at work, he insisted on having his back against a wall so he could see the entire room. His family and friends found it peculiar, but to Gus, it was just common sense. Gus also started ruminating about how to get even with the assailants. He spent hours replaying the events in his head, thinking of all the things he could have done differently, and imagining scenarios where he took down the terrorists single-handedly. It wasn't just a matter of revenge - it was about regaining control over a situation that had left him feeling powerless. As time went on, Gus's behavior began to affect his relationships with those around him. His wife, worried about his increasing paranoia, tried to reassure him that they were safe now. But Gus couldn't shake off the feeling that he had failed in his most important role as a protector - not just of others, but also of himself. He felt like he couldn't deal with even the slightest upset anymore, and the thought sent him spiraling into despair. At work, Gus's colleagues noticed that he was becoming increasingly withdrawn. He would sit at his post for hours without speaking to anyone, his eyes scanning the crowds with an intensity that made them uncomfortable. His managers tried to talk to him about it, but Gus just shrugged it off - what did they know? They hadn't been there that day. It wasn't until Gus's wife sat him down and told him she was worried about losing the man she loved that he realized things had gone too far. The thought of his family giving up on him because of his own fears and doubts was a wake-up call - maybe it was time to get some help. As he sat in the therapist's office, Gus couldn't shake off the feeling that he was weak for seeking help, but he knew he needed to try something. He just hoped it wasn't too late to regain control over his life. Gus glanced around the room, his eyes instinctively searching for an exit route and potential threats - old habits die hard. But as he began to talk about what had brought him there, a glimmer of hope flickered in his eyes - maybe this was the first step towards reclaiming his sense of purpose and self-worth.
